---
title: "Quiz: watershed segmentation of a real image"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The landscape is the gradient magnitude $\|\nabla (G_\sigma * I)\|$ unless stated otherwise; markers are all regional minima, the h-minima, or chosen markers.

---

**Q1.** Why does the watershed of the raw gradient of a noisy image give thousands of regions?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does noise do to a flat region of the gradient?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Inside a flat region the gradient is small but not constant: noise makes it go up and down, and every tiny dip is a regional minimum. Each minimum starts its own basin, so each dip becomes a region.
:::

---

**Q2.** You double $\sigma$. Name one thing that gets better and two that get worse.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Noise, edges, small things.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Better: the noise in the gradient falls (like $1/\sigma^2$), so there are fewer and shallower noise minima. Worse: edges get wider and weaker and their position shifts at corners; nearby edges merge; small objects and thin structures blur away. And the noise minima are still there, only shallower.
:::

---

**Q3.** With $h = 4$ you get the right segmentation. A colleague stretches the contrast of the image by a factor 3 before the watershed. What $h$ should they use?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Depths are differences of heights.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
About 12: the gradient, and with it every depth, is multiplied by 3. (The flooding itself, from fixed markers, would not change: it only compares heights.)
:::

---

**Q4.** What do markers decide, and what does the flooding decide, in a marker-controlled watershed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many, and where.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The markers decide how many regions there are (one per marker) and roughly which object each region is. The flooding decides where the boundaries between them go: on the highest ridges between the markers.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two touching nuclei of equal brightness, each with its own marker. Where does the watershed of the gradient put the boundary between them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Is there an edge between them?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Wherever the two lakes meet in the flat interior: there is no ridge between them, only noise. The split exists (two markers, two regions), but its position is not reliable. The distance transform ([next unit](../ws-distance/lec.qmd)) gives a landscape with a ridge at the neck.
:::

---

**Q6.** A cell's membrane has a gap. Why can the watershed leak through it, while a method that penalises the boundary length (such as a graph cut) closes it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The watershed looks at the highest point on the way; a cut pays for every boundary pixel.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The watershed only asks for the lowest pass between two markers; a gap is a low pass, so water crosses it, however short the gap. A graph cut pays for the length of the boundary: closing the gap with a short straight piece is cheaper than a long detour through the cell, so it closes the gap.
:::

---

**Q7.** What is a hierarchical watershed, and how is the h-minima result related to it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Start from every minimum and merge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Start from the oversegmentation (one region per minimum) and merge neighbouring regions one at a time across their lowest dam (or by another criterion); the merges form a tree. Each level of the tree is a segmentation. Merging in order of the minima's dynamics and stopping at $h$ gives the same regions as h-minima with that $h$.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* By which factor does the noise in $\partial_x (G_\sigma * I)$ fall when $\sigma$ doubles, and by which factor the peak of a sharp edge?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Noise standard deviation $\propto 1/\sigma^2$, edge peak $\propto 1/\sigma$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Noise: by 4 (standard deviation $s/(\sqrt{8\pi}\,\sigma^2)$). Edge peak: by 2 ($J/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma)$ for a sharp step). So the edge-to-noise ratio doubles, but the edges also get twice as wide.
:::
